name: Socratic ignorance ('I know that I know nothing')
plain_explanation: Socrates claimed to know nothing important, and said his only advantage over other supposedly wise men was that he, unlike them, was aware of his own ignorance.
precise_definition: The Socratic doctrine, as reported in the Apology, that human wisdom is 'worth little or nothing,' and that the wisest man is the one who, like Socrates, recognizes the worthlessness of his own wisdom.
why_it_mattered: It reframed philosophy as a lifelong search rather than a possession of settled truths, and gave Socrates his mission (given, he says, by the god) of testing others' claims to wisdom.
historical_origin: Traced by Plato to the story of the Delphic oracle declaring no man wiser than Socrates.
examples: Socrates interrogating a politician, then poets, then artisans, and finding each falls short of the wisdom he or others attributed to him.
competing_positions: The Sophists' claim to teach wisdom or virtue for a fee, which Socrates explicitly rejects and mocks.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Presented by Socrates as a religious duty imposed by the god of Delphi, making his philosophical activity a form of piety rather than the impiety he was charged with.
